passage: On the first cold morning of the term in Toronto, Yosef watched Ms Noa hand back the reading logs. She said the same friendly thing to Ben, whose parents drove him in a big car, and to Mariam, whose coat had a patched elbow. When new Luca, who barely spoke English, put up a hesitant hand, Ms Noa waited and gave him the same full turn as anyone else. Nobody sighed or rolled their eyes. Yosef noticed that his shoulders were relaxed, which they weren't in every classroom. At the end of the day he asked her about the bird picture on the wall, and she answered as if it were the most interesting question of the week.

qa.q: Where was Yosef's school?
qa.a: It was in Toronto.

qa.q: What does Yosef's relaxed body suggest he felt in Ms Noa's class?
qa.a: He felt safe there: his shoulders were relaxed, as he did not in every classroom.

qa.q: What does Ms Noa's behaviour show about fairness?
qa.a: She gave everyone the same friendly words and the same full turn, whatever their background, so fairness looked like a choice she made every time.

qa.q: How might Luca feel when Ms Noa waits for him to finish?
qa.a: Probably more comfortable and safe to keep trying, since nobody sighed or rolled their eyes.

grounding: A child notices a teacher treating every child alike whatever their background and feels safe.

passage: I'm Irawati. At lunch yesterday, Rohan told a joke about people from Asif's religion. It was a mean joke, but the way he told it made everybody laugh, and I laughed too before I even thought. Then I saw Asif. His smile had gone, and he looked down at his lunchbox and started closing it. My stomach went funny. All evening I kept hearing my own laugh. At home I couldn't eat much. This morning I went to Asif and said, "I'm sorry I laughed yesterday. It wasn't funny, it was mean." He shrugged a little. "Okay. Thanks for saying." Next time I won't laugh. I'll say, "That's not funny."

qa.q: Who told the joke at lunch?
qa.a: Rohan told it.

qa.q: Why did Irawati's stomach go funny after the joke?
qa.a: She felt guilty because she had laughed, and she saw Asif's smile vanish and him close his lunchbox.

qa.q: What could Irawati do next time she hears a joke like that?
qa.a: She can avoid laughing and say, "That's not funny," as she plans, and apologise if she slips.

qa.q: How might Asif have felt when Irawati apologised?
qa.a: Probably a little relieved and hurt at once, since he shrugged, said okay and thanked her for saying.

grounding: A child who laughed at a joke about someone's religion feels guilty, apologises and resolves to avoid such jokes.

passage: The rain came down so hard that the school bus was late, and Wasim and Devika crowded under the old peepal tree by the gate with their bags over their heads. "We'll be soaked," Devika grumbled, checking her wet shoes. Wasim didn't answer. He was looking up. Drops raced along every leaf, joined, and fell in silver strings, and the huge trunk seemed to drink it all. "This tree is older than the school," he whispered. "Look at it." Devika looked. On Saturday, her mother gave them a small neem sapling from her nursery, and they planted it by the school wall, patting the earth down with their palms.

qa.q: Where did Wasim and Devika shelter from the rain?
qa.a: They sheltered under the old peepal tree by the gate.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling as he watched the rain fall from the tree?
qa.a: Amazement and wonder; he whispered and could not stop looking up, even though they were getting wet.

qa.q: What small step connected the children to nature after the rain?
qa.a: They planted a neem sapling by the school wall on Saturday. 🙂

qa.q: How does Devika's reaction differ from Wasim's at first?
qa.a: She is worried about being soaked and about her wet shoes, while he is lost in wonder, until she looks up too.

grounding: A child feels awe watching rain and an old tree, and plants a sapling to stay connected to nature.

passage: At lunch break on the hot playground, Kashish saw a thin brown dog lying in the shade by the school gate, panting with its tongue out. The water cooler was empty and the dog's bowl-shaped puddle had dried. Her heart squeezed. She wanted to run straight to it, but she remembered her mother's rule about unknown dogs. Instead she ran to Sachin Bhaiya, the watchman. "The dog is thirsty!" "Good that you told me," he said, and took a steel bowl from his cabin. He filled it and set it a few steps from the dog. Kashish kept her distance and watched it lap. "Can we do this every day?"

qa.q: Where was the dog lying?
qa.a: It was lying in the shade by the school gate.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel on seeing the dog, and why did she not run straight to it?
qa.a: She felt worried for the thirsty dog and wanted to help, but she remembered her mother's rule about unknown dogs, so she told an adult first.

qa.q: What went right in how Kashish helped the dog?
qa.a: She told the watchman first and stayed at a distance while he set the water down, so the dog got help safely. 😊

qa.q: How might Sachin Bhaiya see Kashish's actions?
qa.a: As kind and sensible, since he said it was good she told him.

grounding: A child sees a thirsty stray dog and helps by telling an adult first and putting out water safely.

passage: "Rehana, why are you standing there?" said Zainab, wiping her hands. "The tap is running," Rehana said. "Ammi's washing the pots and it's been running the whole time." "It's always like that." "Can we try a bucket? Then it won't run." Ammi looked over her shoulder. "In my mother's house we kept the tap open all day." "I know, Ammi. But our tank was empty last week, remember?" Rehana said softly. "I could hold the bucket for you." Ammi pursed her lips, then laughed. "All right, all right. Bring the bucket." Zainab smiled. "And can we stop burning the plastic in the yard? It smells so bad." "One thing at a time," said Ammi.

qa.q: Where did Rehana suggest they use a bucket?
qa.a: She suggested it for washing the pots, instead of leaving the tap running.

qa.q: What is Rehana feeling as she stands watching the tap run?
qa.a: She is uneasy about the waste, but she speaks softly so as not to shame her mother.

qa.q: What went well in how Rehana raised the idea, and why?
qa.a: She offered to hold the bucket and reminded Ammi about the empty tank without blaming her, so Ammi agreed with a laugh.

qa.q: How might Ammi see Rehana's suggestion?
qa.a: At first as a change from how her own mother did things, but she is willing after Rehana asks gently, and she pushes the next change to another day.

grounding: A child uneasy about wasted water and burnt plastic suggests a bucket politely, without shaming her family.

passage: "Look, it's the cleaner!" Imran called. A few kids snorted. Wasim bent and picked up a chips packet by the drain. His ears went hot. "It'll take one minute," he muttered. "Why bother? Someone will sweep it," said Imran. "The drain gets blocked when it rains." "Then let it." Wasim dropped the packet into the bin. He didn't smile, but he didn't stop either. Devika, who had been watching from the swing, walked over. "That one's mine," she said, and picked up a paper cup. "Hey!" Imran laughed. "Are you his helper?" Devika shrugged. "Someone has to." Wasim's ears cooled a little.

qa.q: Where was the chips packet that Wasim picked up?
qa.a: It was by the drain.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling when Imran called him the cleaner?
qa.a: Embarrassed, shown by his hot ears, but he still believed picking up litter mattered.

qa.q: What did Wasim do that showed quiet strength?
qa.a: He kept picking up the litter and gave a simple reason, that the drain gets blocked when it rains, without arguing.

qa.q: How might Devika see Wasim's picking up litter?
qa.a: As something worth joining, since she stepped in and picked up a cup while Imran laughed.

grounding: A child laughed at for picking up litter continues quietly and a classmate follows.

passage: Dear diary, I'm Chinmay. Today in class we watched a film about melting ice and hot summers, and now my tummy feels tight. What if things get really bad when I'm grown up? I couldn't finish my dinner. Eshaan bhaiya saw and asked what was wrong. He said sometimes he worries too and that it doesn't mean we're silly. We went to Papa together. Papa said it's understandable to feel that way and that lots of people are working on it. He said we can't fix everything, but we can do small things: switch off fans, carry a cloth bag, plant something. I'm going to start with the bag. I feel a bit less heavy.

qa.q: What did the class watch that upset Chinmay?
qa.a: They watched a film about melting ice and hot summers.

qa.q: Why couldn't Chinmay finish his dinner?
qa.a: He was anxious about what might happen when he grows up, and the worry made his tummy feel tight.

qa.q: What small steps can Chinmay focus on?
qa.a: Things within his control, such as switching off fans, carrying a cloth bag and planting something, after talking to Papa.

qa.q: How does Eshaan bhaiya see Chinmay's worry?
qa.a: As understandable and not silly, since he says he worries sometimes too.

grounding: A child hears about climate change and becomes anxious, then talks to family and chooses small steps.

passage: The bus horn was honking twice, and Arnab dashed down the lane with his bag banging. At the corner Kalyani, the street sweeper, bent over her long broom in the early light, clearing a pile of dry leaves. Last week his class had visited a paddy field, where the farmer had shown them his cracked hands and explained how each grain was planted by hand. Arnab slowed for one second. "Thank you, Kalyani Didi, for keeping the lane clean!" She looked up, surprised, and smiled. He ran on, caught the bus door, and at lunch scraped every last grain from his tiffin, thinking of those cracked hands.

qa.q: What did the farmer show the class at the paddy field?
qa.a: He showed them his cracked hands and explained how each grain was planted by hand.

qa.q: What did Arnab seem to be feeling when he scraped every last grain from his tiffin?
qa.a: Gratitude and respect for the farmer, and perhaps a touch of sadness when he thought of those cracked hands.

qa.q: What small habits show Arnab's respect for people who work with their hands?
qa.a: Stopping to thank Kalyani, even in a rush, and wasting no food at lunch.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel when Arnab thanks her?
qa.a: Surprised and pleased, since she looked up and smiled.

grounding: A child learns how a farmer and a sweeper work, feels respect, and thanks them and wastes less.

passage: I'm Chinmay, and I was at the park with Eshaan when a huge dog came along on a lead. Eshaan stopped and stepped behind the bench. He didn't run. He said, "Let's wait here till they pass." He asked the man at the other end of the lead, from far off, if the dog was friendly. The man said yes, but Eshaan stayed where he was. Then a boy nearby yelled and threw a stick at the dog. Eshaan said, "Don't! He's just a dog." He kept his hands tight around the bench. I don't know exactly how scared he was, but it looked like a lot.

qa.q: Where did Eshaan step when the huge dog came along?
qa.a: He stepped behind the bench.

qa.q: What might Eshaan have been feeling as he held the bench?
qa.a: Probably fear, which is what his tight hands suggest, though Chinmay cannot know for sure.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do to learn more about dogs so fear doesn't turn into cruelty?
qa.a: He can keep his distance, ask adults and learn about how dogs behave.

qa.q: How does Chinmay see Eshaan's reaction?
qa.a: As careful and kind, since Eshaan did not run and told the boy not to hurt the dog, although Chinmay cannot tell exactly how frightened he was.

grounding: A child scared of a big dog keeps his distance and asks first, without being cruel, seen through a friend's eyes.

passage: Monday: Saurabh's test came back with a red 'Fail' at the top. He shoved it deep in his bag, his face hot. It felt as if every single person in the room was looking at him and thinking he was stupid. Tuesday: he ate lunch at the far end of the yard. Chetan found him. "I failed last month's maths," he said, easily. "It was awful." Saurabh stared. "You did?" Following Monday: Saurabh took the test to the teacher. "Which part should I practise?" The teacher pointed to fractions. Saurabh drew a small circle around them and wrote 'practise' beside the circle.

qa.q: What did Saurabh do with the test paper on Monday?
qa.a: He shoved it deep in his bag.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh eat lunch at the far end of the yard?
qa.a: He was ashamed and felt as if the whole class thought he was stupid, so he wanted to hide.

qa.q: How did Saurabh's view of the failed test change by the next Monday?
qa.a: He began to treat it as information about what to practise, and asked the teacher which part needed work. 😊

qa.q: How might Chetan see Saurabh's failed test?
qa.a: As something ordinary that has happened to him too, which is why he mentioned his own failed maths easily.

grounding: A child ashamed of failing a test moves from hiding to treating it as information about what to practise.
